title: Coventry Carol
description: The mothers' lullaby from the Coventry pageant of the Shearmen and Tailors, "Lully lulla thou littell tyne child", in the three parts of its 1591 setting as Thomas Sharp printed them in 1825, with a fourth part of our own, for 2 to 4 singers: the refrain, the three verses, and the refrain again, slow and gentle. The old harmony turns from minor to major on "lulla", on "this day" and on every last "lullay".

credits.words: The women's song from the Pageant of the Shearmen and Tailors, Coventry (as printed by Thomas Sharp, 1825)
credits.tune: The anonymous setting of 1591 (as printed by Thomas Sharp, 1825)
credits.arrangement: The 1591 three-part setting, adapted by Stackapella, with a tenor by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: the song the women sing in the Shearmen and Tailors' pageant of Coventry, anonymous, on the leaf of the pageant's songs dated 13 May 1591 (Robert Croo's text of the pageant itself is dated 14 March 1534 by its colophon); as printed by Thomas Sharp (died 1841), 1825
licence.tune: public domain: the anonymous three-part setting on that leaf, headed with the name Thomas Mawdycke and the date, engraved in facsimile for Thomas Sharp (died 1841) in 1825; the manuscripts burned at Birmingham in 1879 (Hardin Craig's edition, 1902, p. xi), so Sharp's plates are its only source
licence.arrangement: the anonymous 1591 setting's own three parts (public domain: 1591; Sharp's engraved facsimile, 1825, Sharp died 1841), read from the plates and written in modern notes by us (the plates' semibreve as a minim and their minim as the crotchet beat here, so their triple time is 3/4): the 1591 treble is the soprano (the tune), the 1591 tenor the alto, the 1591 bass the bass; the tenor is ours, written under them so the duet (soprano and tenor) and the trio (soprano, tenor and bass) keep each chord's third, which the 1591 trio often leaves open. Changed from the plates, for the song as sung today and for beginners: the refrain is the familiar short one, the 1591 refrain's first line and its own last "lullay" (the plates' refrain runs on through "lullay thou littell tyne child, by by lully lullay" first), sung before verse 1 and again after verse 3 (the plates give it once, before the verses), as The English Carol Book (1923 printing) and Frank Landon Humphreys's Christmas Carols (1900) print it; the tune's "singe" in verse 1 is F sharp where the plates print F with no sign (the same cadence has its sharp printed in the refrain and in verses 2 and 3), and in verse 3 its "for" and "And" are G where the plates print F, against the plates' own E-flat and G minor chords (verse 1 has G at the same places); the alto sings one note a syllable where the plates' tenor moves in two quick notes: B-flat on verse 3's "for" and "nor", D on "this" and "and", C (the second note, so the chord is E-flat with its sixth) on "we", "do", "rag-" and "owne", and D on "tiné" (the plates' B-flat and C), its "whom" (a semibreve under the tune's dotted "whom we") is split to the tune's syllables, it sings D, not the plates' F, on "This", "His" and "For" after the breath (the plates leap a tritone there from B natural), and D, not the plates' F natural, on the second "by" at the end of verses 1 and 3, where the F sounds against the tune's F sharp (the plates' own refrain has D there); the plates' tenor writes "O" (verse 1) and "sight" (verse 2) shorter than the treble and bass do, and they are sung here at the treble's length; the bass sings G3, an octave above the plates' G2, on "lulla", "too", "king" and "me", so it doesn't leap down and back an octave inside the line; every part's line end gives up a beat (three quarters before "This", "His" and "For") for a breath; the last chord of verse 2, an open G and D in 1591, has our tenor's B natural, as the other verses end major; the tenor (ours) is fixed by the choral review so every chord has its third at 2 and 3 singers: E-flat 3 under the C minor of "lul-ly" before "by" in verses 1 and 3 (as in the refrain), A3, B-flat 3 and D4 under "may we do" and "his rag-ing", E-flat 4 then C4 (a D7 resolving to the B natural) under "-dren to", and E-flat 3 then D3 under "nor singe"; "tyne" is sung as the plates' underlay sets it, on one note (Sharp's text, p. 113, prints "tiné"); accepted exceptions, all in the 1591 notes (plate 117): the soprano and bass in parallel fifths on "say nor" (A4 over D3 to G4 over C3) and in octaves by contrary motion into "ly" before "by" in verses 1 and 3 (G4 over G3 to C5 over C3); the alto's line (the 1591 tenor) swinging by thirds, and its leap down from F4 to B-flat 3 on "nor" without a step back; the bass's falls of a fifth to C3 and G2 at every cadence; the duet's octaves B-flat on "Herod" and G on "for" in verse 3 (each keeps the chord's third, and any other tenor note there makes fifths or unisons with the 1591 bass); and our tenor's leaps into those thirds (up from E-flat 3 after "ly", D3 up to B-flat 3 after the breath following "singe"), each turning back by step or third.
licence.source: Thomas Sharp, A Dissertation on the Pageants or Dramatic Mysteries Anciently Performed at Coventry (Coventry: Merridew and Son, 1825): the words of "Song II" on pp. 113 and 114 under "Theise songes belonge to the Taylors & Shearemens Pagant. The first and the laste the shepheards singe and the second or middlemost the women singe", and the music, "Song II", on the engraved plates numbered 116 and 117 ("The treble", "The tenor", "The basse", in parts, in the old notation, one flat, the tune in the C clef on the first line), its three verses each set out in full; in G minor (one flat) as printed and written here in G minor, 3/4; words as printed on pp. 113 and 114, "þu" and "þis" written "thou" and "this"; read from the scan of a copy digitized by Google (the plates at full resolution) at archive.org/details/adissertationonthepageants (pages n142 to n148), checked against the University of Toronto copy at archive.org/details/dissertationonpa00sharuoft (page/n264 and n266); the familiar refrain and verse order compared with The English Carol Book, second series, ed. Martin Shaw and Percy Dearmer (London: Mowbray, 1923), No. 38, p. 83 ("Tune 1591"), archive.org/details/englishcarolbook00dear/page/n18, and Christmas Carols, selected by Frank Landon Humphreys (copyright 1900), p. 41, archive.org/details/christmascarols00humpgoog/page/n45; neither book's harmony is used
